In [[first-order arithmetic]], the '''induction principles''', '''bounding principles''', and '''least number principles''' are three related families of first-order principles, which may or may not hold in [[Non-standard model of arithmetic|nonstandard models of arithmetic]]. These principles are often used in [[reverse mathematics]] to calibrate the axiomatic strength of theorems.

==Definitions==

Informally, for a [[First-order logic|first-order]] [[Well-formed formula|formula]] of arithmetic <math>\varphi(x)</math> with one free variable, the '''induction principle for <math>\varphi</math>''' expresses the validity of [[mathematical induction]] over <math>\varphi</math>, while the '''least number principle for <math>\varphi</math>''' asserts that if <math>\varphi</math> has a [[Witness (mathematics)|witness]], it has a least one. For a formula <math>\psi(x,y)</math> in two free variables, the '''bounding principle for <math>\psi</math>''' states that, for a fixed ''bound'' <math>k</math>, if for every <math>n < k</math> there is <math>m_n</math> such that <math>\psi(n,m_n)</math>, then we can find a bound on the <math>m_n</math>'s.

Formally, the '''induction principle for <math>\varphi</math>''' is the sentence:<ref name=":0">{{Cite book|last1=Hájek|first1=Petr|title=Metamathematics of First-Order Arithmetic|last2=Pudlák|first2=Pavel|publisher=Association for Symbolic Logic c/- Cambridge University Press|year=2016|isbn=978-1-107-16841-1|oclc=1062334376}}</ref>

: <math>\mathsf{I}\varphi: \quad \big[ \varphi(0) \land \forall x \big( \varphi(x) \to \varphi(x+1) \big) \big] \to \forall x\ \varphi (x)</math>

There is a similar '''[[Mathematical induction#Complete (strong) induction|strong induction]] principle for <math>\varphi</math>''':<ref name=":0" />

: <math>\mathsf{I}'\varphi: \quad \forall x \big[ \big( \forall y<x\ \ \varphi(y) \big) \to \varphi(x) \big] \to \forall x\ \varphi (x)</math>

The '''least number principle for <math>\varphi</math>''' is the sentence:<ref name=":0" />

: <math>\mathsf{L}\varphi: \quad \exists x\ \varphi (x) \to \exists x' \big( \varphi (x') \land \forall y < x'\ \, \lnot \varphi(y) \big)</math>

Finally, the '''bounding principle for <math>\psi</math>''' is the sentence:<ref name=":0" />

: <math>\mathsf{B}\psi: \quad \forall u \big[ \big( \forall x < u\ \, \exists y\ \, \psi(x,y) \big) \to \exists v\ \, \forall x < u\ \, \exists y < v\ \, \psi(x,y) \big]</math>

More commonly, we consider these principles not just for a single formula, but for a class of formulae in the [[arithmetical hierarchy]]. For example, <math>\mathsf{I}\Sigma_2</math> is the [[axiom schema]] consisting of <math>\mathsf{I}\varphi</math> for every <math>\Sigma_2</math> formula <math>\varphi(x)</math> in one free variable.

==Nonstandard models==

It may seem that the principles <math>\mathsf{I}\varphi</math>, <math>\mathsf{I}'\varphi</math>, <math>\mathsf{L}\varphi</math>, <math>\mathsf{B}\psi</math> are trivial, and indeed, they hold for all formulae <math>\varphi</math>, <math>\psi</math> in the [[Natural number|standard model of arithmetic]] <math>\mathbb{N}</math>. However, they become more relevant in nonstandard models. Recall that a nonstandard model of arithmetic has the form <math>\mathbb{N} + \mathbb{Z} \cdot K</math> for some linear order <math>K</math>. In other words, it consists of an initial copy of <math>\mathbb{N}</math>, whose elements are called ''finite'' or ''standard'', followed by many copies of <math>\mathbb{Z}</math> arranged in the shape of <math>K</math>, whose elements are called ''infinite'' or ''nonstandard''.

Now, considering the principles <math>\mathsf{I}\varphi</math>, <math>\mathsf{I}'\varphi</math>, <math>\mathsf{L}\varphi</math>, <math>\mathsf{B}\psi</math> in a nonstandard model <math>\mathcal{M}</math>, we can see how they might fail. For example, the hypothesis of the induction principle <math>\mathsf{I}\varphi</math> only ensures that <math>\varphi(x)</math> holds for all elements in the ''standard'' part of <math>\mathcal{M}</math> - it may not hold for the nonstandard elements, who can't be reached by iterating the successor operation from zero. Similarly, the bounding principle <math>\mathsf{B}\psi</math> might fail if the bound <math>u</math> is nonstandard, as then the (infinite) collection of <math>y</math> could be [[Cofinal (mathematics)|cofinal]] in <math>\mathcal{M}</math>.

==Relations between the principles==
[[File:Induction, bounding, least number principles.png|thumb|The relations between the induction, bounding and least number principles.|354x354px]]

The following relations hold between the principles (over the weak base theory <math>\mathsf{PA}^- +\mathsf{I}\Sigma_0</math>):<ref name=":0" /><ref>{{Citation|last1=Paris|first1=J.B.|chapter=Σn-Collection Schemas in Arithmetic|date=1978|chapter-url=http://dx.doi.org/10.1016/s0049-237x(08)72003-2|title=Logic Colloquium '77|pages=199–209|publisher=Elsevier|isbn=978-0-444-85178-9|access-date=2021-04-14|last2=Kirby|first2=L.A.S.|doi=10.1016/s0049-237x(08)72003-2|chapter-url-access=subscription}}</ref>

* <math>\mathsf{I}'\varphi \equiv \mathsf{L}\lnot\varphi</math> for every formula <math>\varphi</math>;
* <math>\mathsf{I}\Sigma_n \equiv \mathsf{I}\Pi_n \equiv \mathsf{I}'\Sigma_n \equiv \mathsf{I}'\Pi_n \equiv \mathsf{L}\Sigma_n \equiv \mathsf{L}\Pi_n</math>;
* <math>\mathsf{I}\Sigma_{n+1} \implies \mathsf{B}\Sigma_{n+1} \implies \mathsf{I}\Sigma_n</math>, and both implications are strict;
* <math>\mathsf{B}\Sigma_{n+1} \equiv \mathsf{B}\Pi_n \equiv \mathsf{L}\Delta_{n+1}</math>;
* <math>\mathsf{L}\Delta_n \implies \mathsf{I}\Delta_n</math>, but it is not known if this reverses.

Over <math>\mathsf{PA}^- +\mathsf{I}\Sigma_0 + \mathsf{exp}</math>, [[Theodore Slaman|Slaman]] proved that <math>\mathsf{B}\Sigma_n \equiv \mathsf{L}\Delta_n \equiv \mathsf{I}\Delta_n</math>.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Slaman|first=Theodore A.|date=2004-08-01|title=<math>\Sigma_n</math>-bounding and <math>\Delta_n</math>-induction|journal=[[Proceedings of the American Mathematical Society]]|volume=132|issue=8|pages=2449|doi=10.1090/s0002-9939-04-07294-6|issn=0002-9939|doi-access=free}}</ref>

==Reverse mathematics==

The induction, bounding and least number principles are commonly used in [[reverse mathematics]] and [[second-order arithmetic]]. For example, <math>\mathsf{I}\Sigma_1</math> is part of the definition of the subsystem <math>\mathsf{RCA}_0</math> of second-order arithmetic. Hence, <math>\mathsf{I}'\Sigma_1</math>, <math>\mathsf{L}\Sigma_1</math> and <math>\mathsf{B}\Sigma_1</math> are all theorems of <math>\mathsf{RCA}_0</math>. The subsystem <math>\mathsf{ACA}_0</math> proves all the principles <math>\mathsf{I}\varphi</math>, <math>\mathsf{I}'\varphi</math>, <math>\mathsf{L}\varphi</math>, <math>\mathsf{B}\psi</math> for [[Arithmetical hierarchy|arithmetical]] <math>\varphi</math>, <math>\psi</math>. The infinite pigeonhole principle is known to be equivalent to <math>\mathsf{B}\Pi_1</math> and <math>\mathsf{B}\Sigma_2</math> over <math>\mathsf{RCA}_0</math>.<ref name=":1">{{cite thesis|last=Hirst|first=Jeffry|date=August 1987|title=Combinatorics in Subsystems of Second Order Arithmetic|type=PhD|publisher=Pennsylvania State University}}</ref>
